title: National Dental Nurse Day 2026: marking a turning point
html:
As we celebrate National Dental Nurse Day, Fiona Ellwood discusses the contrast of the dental nursing profession’s growing influence with persistent questions about pay, training and recognition.

Dental nursing is entering a decisive period. The profession is now the largest registrable group on the General Dental Council register, with numbers exceeding 68,000 after a reported 5.4% rise. Yet growth has not resolved the pressures felt by many nurses: burnout, limited earning potential, workforce strain and a sense that their contribution is still too often overlooked.

For Fiona Ellwood, speaking as the British Dental Nurse Society marks its 10th anniversary, the central challenge is to turn that visibility into meaningful progression.

A year of celebration and scrutiny

The year has carried particular symbolic weight. It marked two decades since the register opened to dental nurses, with mandatory registration following the closure of the gateway period in 2008. It also culminated in the society’s anniversary conference, which brought together dental nurses and senior figures from across the profession to discuss the past, present and future of dental nursing.

Ellwood described the response as overwhelmingly positive. ‘I don’t think I’ve ever felt so much pride in all my life,’ she said.

A panel involving dental nurses, the GDC, the British Dental Association (BDA) and the chief dental officer for England created space for both celebration and direct questioning. One comment in particular stayed with her: Simon Thackeray said he had rarely seen a room of dental nurses so ‘positive and constructive’ and so determined to work together.

That optimism matters because it sits alongside serious concerns. A survey referenced by Ellwood suggested that 92% of responding dental nurses had experienced burnout. Surveys continue to monitor what influences retention, with money no longer necessarily the sole or leading factor. Other influences such as workload, recognition, development and the quality of support all matter.

New opportunities in dental nursing need practical support

One of the year’s most significant developments was clarification that dental nurses can apply fluoride varnish in scheduled care. It offered a glimpse of greater autonomy and a possible role in prevention, including the prospect of generating 0.5 of a UDA. But the announcement also exposed uncertainty across the workforce about what scheduled care involves and who can delegate it.

‘We had to spend quite a bit of time reassuring nurses about what the change meant,’ Ellwood said.

Ellwood is clear that dental hygienists and dental therapists cannot simply refer or delegate the duty to dental nurses. The bigger question is whether practices can make the time and space for nurses to use skills they have trained for.

‘There’s still too much red tape and bureaucracy around some of the work that we could be doing,’ she said. Without a rethink of service design, qualifications may sit unused.

This is where skill mix becomes more than a policy slogan. New models of care affect the whole dental team, not only dentists. Urgent care pathways, changes to contracts and increased use of skill mix can place extra demands on nurses, administrators and those responsible for infection prevention and instrument processing. Teams need protected time, training and support to adapt safely.

Training and registration remain live issues

The society welcomed a change allowing a dental nurse to spend up to 12 months in work before enrolling on a course. Even so, it had advocated for a six-month period, arguing that a year is too long. The difference reflects a wider tension between flexibility for employers and the need to ensure that new entrants move promptly into structured training.

Registration administration has also caused concern. Ellwood pointed to the difficult rollout of MyGDC at a time when many dental care professionals were seeking to upload CPD, pay indemnity and complete other requirements. The GDC has pledged to improve the MyGDC platform going forward, but uncertainty over compliance can cause an acute impact for a workforce already under pressure.

The planned rise in the annual retention fee for 2027 is another flashpoint. Dental nurses pay the same fee as other dental care professional groups while often having lower earning capacity.

‘We know we won’t see the pay increase for nurses to be able to manage that increase,’ Ellwood said. The society continues to argue for differentiated categories, informed by the way CPD is structured, so that costs better reflect the realities of different roles.

A platform for progression

Alongside its advocacy work, the British Dental Nurse Society is focused on showing what progression can look like. Its annual awards, announced today on National Dental Nurse Day (22 November), recognise inspirational nurses, students, early- and long-career professionals, mentors, charitable leads and treatment coordinators. The date commemorates the first dental nursing examination in 1943, when 135 of 175 candidates passed.

The society has contributed to work on professionalism, fitness to practise, discrimination in dentistry and antimicrobial resistance, as well as raising concerns about sexual misconduct. It has also launched a gateway into dental therapy with the University of Lincolnshire: a year of intensive science study designed to give eligible dental nurses a direct route into a dental therapy course when they do not have conventional UCAS qualifications or A levels.

That pathway captures Ellwood’s broader ambition. Dental nursing should not be regarded as a static role, but as a profession with viable routes into advanced practice, education, leadership and other parts of the dental team. For that ambition to be credible, though, opportunity must be matched by proper remuneration, workforce planning and respect.

A renewed identity

The end of the anniversary year also brings a symbolic victory. After a long-running trademark dispute, the organisation has regained the name under which it was first established: the British Dental Nurse Society. Its purpose and values have not changed, Ellwood says, but reclaiming the name feels like a fitting close to the first decade.

The next chapter will bring new leadership and a continued commitment to education, advocacy and professional recognition. The anniversary message is clear: dental nurses have a stronger collective voice and expect it to be heard.
